PMGT1852 Week 13

PMGT1852 Week 13 - The Secrets to Closing: Review, Define, Evaluate, End, Debrief

Overview

A meeting that just stops leaves its results unowned and unactioned. This week covers:

• The questions a meeting must answer when it closes.

• The five-step closing sequence: Review, Define, Evaluate, End, Debrief.

• Checking participants' personal objectives at the close.

• Winning commitment to the decisions (polling the jury).

• Clearing the Issues list and the Actions list.

• Three types of communication plan.

• Evaluating the session, spoken and written.

• Ending the session and debriefing with the sponsor.

Key Concepts

The questions a closing must answer

• What did we accomplish?

• What decisions did we make?

• How can we tell others about the session?

• How will it be documented?

• What happens when we leave the room?

• Who is responsible for making it happen?

• When do we come back together? What will we do then?

Consensus

Consensus is defined at the start of the meeting as "I can live with it, and I will support it." It is not unanimity of preference: people do not have to prefer the decision, only to be able to live with it and support it.

Walk the walls

To review the group's work, point at the results of each step as they appear on the walls and go through them item by item.

The secret of the Actions list

Assign actions only to people who are present, and let each person set their own date.

Frameworks and Formulas

The five-step closing sequence

Review - the activities carried out, the participants' objectives, and the parking boards (issues, decisions, actions).

Define - what may be communicated outside about this meeting.

Evaluate - the value and results of the meeting.

End - remind everyone of the next steps and formally close.

Debrief - with the sponsor, covering strengths and improvements.

Step 1: reviewing activities and personal objectives

Walk through the agenda item by item, or "walk the walls". For each personal objective captured at the start, ask "Was this objective fulfilled?": tick the fulfilled ones, circle the unfulfilled ones, discuss what should happen to the circled items, and put those follow-ups on the Actions list.

Step 2A: confirming commitment to decisions

(The decisions have been captured on the Decisions, Issues and Actions lists.)

Simple review: "Does this list fairly portray the decisions we made? Any others?"

Document benefits: number each decision and use a vivid, open-ended question to list its benefits. Why: everyone then shares a clear understanding of the results and a common vision of the value gained, and participants can explain the reasons for the decision to other people.

Identify barriers and strategies: internal, external or other barriers; a strategy to prevent each barrier from having its effect; then who leads each strategy and by when.

Barrier

Strategy

Who

When

Internal barrier (example row)

Management briefing on recommendations and benefits

Robert

within 3 weeks

Internal barrier (example row)

Supervisor briefing to define interview-training needs and select three supervisors as an HR advisory team

Sandra

within 6 weeks

Polling the jury:

◦ At the start of the meeting, define consensus as "I can live with it, and I will support it", and say that consensus will be asked for at the end.

◦ After reviewing the decisions, benefits, barriers and strategies, ask each participant: "Can you live with and support these decisions?"

◦ If someone raises a concern, ask: "What is the minimum amount of change you would recommend so this is something you can live with and support?"

◦ For milder concerns, ask: "Will these concerns prevent you from living with and supporting the solution?"

◦ If changes are proposed, suggest a time limit and ask whether the group wants to discuss them; once resolved, gain consensus from everyone.

Step 2B: clearing the Issues list

For each issue on the Issues list, work through this decision path:

• "Have we covered it?" - yes: go to the next item.

• no: "Do we need to cover it?" - no: go to the next item.

• yes: "Do we need to cover it now?" - yes: set a time limit and facilitate the discussion; no: move the item to the Actions list.

Step 2C: dealing with the Actions list

• Review each item and remind the group that the person an action is assigned to is responsible for getting it done (they need not do it personally).

• Assigning an action to someone who is not present is not appropriate. An item can be given to a person with the authority to delegate it to an absent person.

• Ask for volunteers or nominations, and let the person themselves set the completion date.

• Tip: ask them to sign their acceptance if they are willing.

Step 2 (Define): communication plans, three types

Simple list - a one-column chart "Items to Communicate", produced with an open question such as: "Imagine one of your people asks, 'So, what did you all do?'"

Dual list - two columns: "Items to Communicate" and "Items not to Communicate" (content that is sensitive or not appropriate to share yet).

Communication plan matrix - five columns:

Audience

Information

Who

Vehicle

When

The groups who need the information (for example hiring managers, employees)

What that audience needs (for example a summary of the new process, or detailed instructions)

The person responsible for making the communication

Email, hard-copy report, presentation

The date by which the communication should occur

Step 3: evaluating the session

Every meeting should collect both positive and negative feedback - what to keep doing and what to change.

• Spoken: 1) round-robin for what people liked; 2) random order for improvement suggestions; 3) a show of hands for support for each suggestion.

• Written: an evaluation form rated Excellent / Good / OK / Poor, in three blocks:

Block

Items rated

Session

content; comprehensiveness; pace; time allocation; overall

Facilitator

understanding of process; ability to facilitate the group; pace; responsiveness to questions; sensitivity to group needs; overall

Performance

how well objectives were met; likelihood of positive change; personal benefit; overall

Plus written comments: the most valuable and the least valuable topics; how to improve; and one or two sentences on the overall benefit and why.

Step 4: ending the session

Thank the participants and remind them of the role this session plays in the overall goal.

Remind them of the next steps: who keeps the meeting record and what happens next; when and how the results will be distributed; and the place, date, time and purpose of the next meeting.

Formally close the meeting.

Step 5: debriefing with the sponsor

Discuss the process and the results: How well were the session objectives met? How well did participants respond? How sufficient are the deliverables? What follow-up activities are needed?

Worked Examples

Barriers and strategies (hiring-process case)

The group lists the barriers that could stop its recommendations from being implemented, and pairs each with a strategy, an owner and a date - as in the table above: Robert takes the management briefing within 3 weeks, and Sandra takes the supervisor briefing (which also selects three supervisors as an HR advisory team) within 6 weeks. The table itself is the deliverable: a barrier without an owner and a date is only a concern.

A communication plan matrix for the same case

The audiences are the groups who must act on the new hiring process - hiring managers and employees. Hiring managers need a summary of the new process and the decisions behind it; employees need detailed instructions for their part of it. For each audience the plan names the person responsible, the vehicle (email, hard-copy report or presentation) and the date by which the communication should occur.

How closing connects to the rest of the session

The close is where the opening's promises are settled: the personal objectives collected when participants were first involved are ticked or circled here, and the parking boards set up at the start are cleared here - decisions confirmed, issues resolved or parked onto the actions list, and actions assigned to the people in the room.

Patterns that run through the whole session:

• The big view of a checkpoint plays the same role as Excite in the opening: it returns every step to the meeting goal.

• Vivid, open-ended starting questions in the participants' own language are used when involving participants, gathering facts, generating ideas, listing the benefits of decisions, and building the communication plan.

• "Say what you like first, then how to make it better" appears when redirecting a negative comment, when groups review each other's flip charts, when commenting on reported results, and when giving feedback.

• Strengths are collected in round-robin order; improvement suggestions in random order.
